chapters.title: Half Past Five
chapters.segment_text:
## Chapter 1 — Half Past Five

The woman came up the back stairs at ten to five with a navy coat over her arm, and asked whether they could take it up an inch and a half.

Alison looked at the clock that had been on that wall since before she came, and said they could.

Nobody had told her, and that was the whole of it. And still she had come up the back stairs the way women had come up the back stairs since 1904, because the fourth floor did alterations and she wanted a coat taking up.

"You're not shutting, are you," the woman said, in the voice of somebody who had read something and decided it was about a different shop.

"We're open till half five," Alison said, which was true, and was the only true thing she could manage.

She put her on the box in front of the three-way mirror. The woman stood the way they all stood, chin up, arms out from her sides like a scarecrow apologising. Alison knelt. Her knees took a second to agree, the way they did now. She turned the hem under and pinned it and stood back and looked, and it was an inch and a half. You knelt down and you pinned it and you let her watch herself in the mirror while you did.

"That's better," the woman said. "Isn't that better."

"It'll hang now," said Alison.

The machine had a lot number on it — a small orange sticker under the balance wheel, LOT 114, put there by a young man from the auctioneers who had said *lovely old thing* about a Singer that had outrun three managers. Alison unpicked, pressed, turned it and ran the seam, and the machine did exactly what it was asked and nothing more.

Forty minutes. She pressed it twice, because a coat is worth two pressings, and put it on a hanger and brought it out.

"What do I owe you?"

"Nothing today."

"Don't be daft."

"Nothing today," Alison said. "Go on."

And the woman, who had a bus to catch, went, calling something over her shoulder about coming back at Christmas with a skirt.

At half past five the lights went off in the lift lobby, and somebody in the stockroom was crying and would not want it known. Alison put her scissors and her good tape measure in her bag, because they were hers, and left the rest.

On the wall by the door were the hooks, and on hers a strip of masking tape with HOYLE on it in biro, in her own hand, written in 2001. She got a thumbnail under the corner. It came away in one piece, which surprised her. She put it in her pocket.

Then she turned off the light over the bench.

The room did not go dark. It stayed exactly as it was — the tables, the mirror, the chalk dust in the boards — because it was a north window, and it had always been the window.
chapters.cliffhanger: There is a table standing empty in the Lantern that nobody has wanted for two years.

chapters.title: What She Was Worth
chapters.segment_text:
## Chapter 2 — What She Was Worth

The letter came with the second post, which meant she was in, because she was in now.

It thanked her for twenty-six years in a font chosen by somebody in an office she had never seen, and explained, in a paragraph she read three times, that the enhanced part was discretionary and had been exercised in her favour. At the bottom it said twenty-one thousand five hundred and seventy pounds.

She put the kettle on.

She had not meant to do the division. But the envelope was in her hand and there was a biro from a bookmaker's she had never been in, and by the time the kettle clicked off she had written 21,570 divided by 26 down the side of the envelope in her mother's handwriting, which is to say her own.

Eight hundred and twenty-nine and something. Call it eight hundred and thirty.

Eight hundred and thirty pounds for a year. For the year she took up eleven bridesmaids in a fortnight and finished the last one at ten past midnight. For the year Gary went, when she came in at half eight every morning and did the work and said nothing, and Pauline said nothing either, correctly.

Then she was annoyed with herself, which took about an hour and did not get her anywhere.

The phone went at four, when the sun got round to the front room, being a first-floor flat over what had been the Co-op.

"Well," said Sylvia. "What are you going to do now, then."

"I'm having a think."

"A think." Her mother left it exactly where she had put it. "You've never had a think in your life. You've a lad in Glasgow and a machine in the spare room and you're fifty-two."

"Fifty-two's not —"

"I know what fifty-two is. I've been it. Have you got money?"

"I've got money."

"Well, then," said Sylvia, in a tone that closed the subject and did not close it at all.

She brought the machine through after tea. It weighed more than a person expects and less than her back believed, and she set it on the kitchen table because there was nowhere else, and the bread board went on the side by the toaster where it did not belong.

She did not sew anything. She sat with the letter and a cup of tea going cold and did not sew anything.

At eleven she got up to go to bed and stopped in the doorway.

The Singer sat under the kitchen light with its wheel and its plate and its long black neck, plugged into nothing. She looked at it the way you look at a horse in a hallway. A good horse. An animal with no business where it was and no way of getting out.
chapters.cliffhanger: The table is under the worst of the draught and the best of the light.

chapters.title: The Lantern
chapters.segment_text:
## Chapter 3 — The Lantern

She went down on the Thursday to look, which is what she told herself on the way.

It had been the Market Hall on the deeds since 1877 and the Lantern in every mouth in the town since about 1950, on account of the eleven glazed lanterns down the spine of the roof, which let down a light no architect since has managed to buy. It smelt of pastry and cut keys and cardboard and cold stone. The columns had been touched up in four different greens by four different men, each of whom had been certain he had matched it.

The empty pitch was by the north door. Thirty-one pitches, twenty-two let, and this one standing empty since a fortnight before the first lockdown.

"Draught's shocking," said Hilary Ashworth, who had arrived beside her without any noise at all. "That door's a nuisance from November."

"It's the best light in the building."

Hilary looked at her.

"It is," she said.

The table was deal, scarred all over, with a bit of somebody's chewing gum under the near edge gone the colour and hardness of a shirt button. On the front board, under forty years of hands, was a ghost sign in signwriter's script: T. CRABTREE & SON · NOTHING OVER 50p.

"Seventy-two pound a week," Hilary said. "All in. That's your leccy, your bins, insurance for the building, not for your stock. There's a leak over pitch seven and everything's under there in a bucket."

"What's the notice?"

"Month either way." She had a ring of keys on her belt that hung to her knee. Alison counted them later, over months, without meaning to: thirty-one. "You'd be sat next to Kelly's coffee. She'll talk at you, but she's no trouble."

Alison did not remember agreeing. She remembered her mouth saying go on, then, which is what you say to a child offering you a sweet, and the whole of it taking less time than a hem.

She scrubbed the table on Friday morning with a bucket and a green pad and the water came off the colour of tea. She emptied it and did it again and it came off the colour of tea again. She stopped after that, on the grounds that a table has a right to some of its own history, and dried it with a towel from home, and the wood came up warm and pale and shocked, like a face out of a scarf.

Then there was nothing to do.

She stood behind it at four o'clock with her hands flat on it. Kelly's chalkboard said CAMOMILLE. Bernie Fazakerley was telling a customer something about her sister the customer had not asked to know. Above her the eleven lanterns let their light down the way they had done for a hundred and forty-nine years — over her, and her table, and her hands.

And every soul in that building was looking at her, kindly, and had already decided how long she would last.
chapters.cliffhanger: The first customer comes at nine minutes past ten, and she is not ready.

chapters.title: A Knee
chapters.segment_text:
## Chapter 4 — A Knee

The first customer came at nine minutes past ten and Alison was not ready, and thought afterwards that she never would have been.

She was young, twenty-six or so, in a coat too thin for the hall, holding a Co-op bag with both hands the way you hold a thing that has got heavier than what is in it. She stood at the corner of the table a moment, not quite arrived.

"Are you doing repairs?"

"I am."

"It's only —" She stopped, and started again, and Alison could hear the rehearsal in it, the sentence built in a kitchen and carried down Corn Street. "It's his school trousers. Both knees have gone. I bought them six weeks since, in July, for starting back, and he's been in them four days."

"Let's have a look."

Grey polyester, age eight, both knees out the way they go — not a tear, a scuff and then a hole, from a boy going down on tarmac at speed because he is eight and the world is worth it. There was a second pair in the bag with one knee gone.

"I've tried patches. Off the internet. They come off in the wash."

"They do."

"I've no more uniform money till —" and she stopped again and looked at the table, and Alison looked at the trousers, because there are moments when the kindest place in the world to put your eyes is on the work.

"I'll put a proper patch in behind and darn over the top," Alison said. "Nothing's invisible on a knee. But it'll go through to Christmas, and when he goes through it again, and he will, you bring them back and I'll do it again."

"How much?"

And there it was. She had thought about this for a week and a half and had a piece of paper at home with numbers on it, crossed out and written again, and not one of them arrived. What arrived was four.

"Four pound."

"For all three knees?"

"For all three knees."

The woman got her purse out and paid in coins, and one of them was a fifty, and Alison did not look at it and did not say anything about it.

She did the work while she waited, because Kelly had a chair going spare and it was nine minutes past ten. Twenty minutes a knee. She did them the way she would have done a lining on the fourth floor, and she hated herself for about an hour afterwards — four pound, four pound, a woman of my age — and then somewhere in the afternoon she stopped, and did not start again.

The young woman folded the bag over and said thank you twice and went.

At the north door she stopped. She looked back down the hall — past Kelly, past the coffee, at the table, and at Alison behind it — for about as long as it takes to read a sign.

Then she went out into Corn Street, and the door swung, and let the draught in.
chapters.cliffhanger: The woman at the trimmings stall has watched her all morning and not said a word.

chapters.title: The Zip
chapters.segment_text:
## Chapter 5 — The Zip

The jacket came in on Saturday over the arm of a woman of sixty-three, who put it down on the table like a cat she was proud of.

"Nineteen ninety-four," she said. "I've had it longer than I had my husband and I've been fonder of it."

Black leather gone soft as a glove, and a smell in it Alison knew — leather and petrol and the inside of somebody's garage in the eighties. The zip had gone at the bottom stop. The stop itself, pulled clean off, so the whole front parted at the hem like a curtain.

"I only need it so it fastens. I'm not fussy."

"You're a bit fussy," Alison said, "or you'd have chucked it."

The woman laughed and said, "Aye, well."

She had started again in June. Thirty-one years off it — a husband, two kids, a mortgage, a knee — and then a fella at the club had a Bonneville going for less than a decent settee, and she was out on the tops at seven on a Tuesday morning with the mist lying in the valley below her like milk in a bowl.

"Does your family not mind?"

"Our Lee thinks it's brilliant. He's been on the back." A pause. She straightened the collar of her own coat on Alison's table. "I've not told our Rachel."

"Right."

"She'd worry."

"She would."

"She'd be right to." The woman looked at her. "I'll tell her when I've had it a twelvemonth and nowt's happened, and then it's a story instead of a row."

Alison, who had not told her own son several things, said nothing at all, and got on.

She wanted a heavy-gauge zip, and there was one place in the building that had one. Which meant crossing the hall. Which meant Sonia Aktar.

She had said good morning to Sonia every day for three days and had had a nod for it, which in Ravensgate is a contract.

Aktar's Trimmings was pitch 4 and had been Aktar's Trimmings since 1979. Drawers to the ceiling, labelled in two alphabets in a hand that had got smaller as the years went on. Sonia was thirty-eight and watched everything in that hall and said about a third of it.

"Number eight, open-end, black," Alison said. "Twenty-four inch if you've got it. It's for leather."

Sonia looked at her for a second longer than the sentence needed. Then she turned and opened a drawer without reading it and laid the zip on the counter.

"Twenty-two," she said. "It'll want shortening at the top."

"I know."

"I know you know."

And she took the zip and ran it flat along the brass yard-measure screwed to her counter — worn down to a shine at thirty-six inches by seventy years of thumbs — and her own thumb came down on the shine, without her looking, the way a thumb does when it has been coming home to the same place all its life.
chapters.cliffhanger: Bernie Fazakerley does not take money off anybody in their first week.

chapters.title: Her Mother's Raincoat
chapters.segment_text:
## Chapter 6 — Her Mother's Raincoat

Sunday, so the hall was shut, and she went up to Weaver's Rise with a tin of biscuits nobody had asked for.

The flat was warden-assisted, which Sylvia pronounced like a diagnosis, and had a view to the crematorium, which Sylvia described as handy, and had done, without varying it, since 2011.

"You've brought biscuits."

"I have."

"I've biscuits."

"Well, now you've more."

They had tea. Sylvia gave her the week. Bowls on Tuesday, in which a woman called Doreen had done something with the mat that would be discussed until Christmas. The committee, from which Sylvia had been asked to step down in the spring and about which she was serene in a way that fooled nobody.

"And you," Sylvia said, "are still having a think."

"I've took a table. In the Lantern."

Her mother put her cup down.

"By the north door," Alison said. "Seventy-two pound a week."

"Crabtree's old spot."

"That's it."

Sylvia looked out at the crematorium. "Well," she said. "You'll want a fan heater."

The raincoat was on the hook in the hall where it had been every Sunday of Alison's adult life. Beige, 1988, from a shop on Corn Street that no longer exists. Sylvia had bought it the year Alison did her City and Guilds. Thirty-eight years of Ravensgate rain had taken it to the weight of paper. When you lifted it off the hook it did not swing. It went with you, all of it at once, like something asleep.

Alison turned the cuff over. It had gone through, both sides, at the fold where a wrist bends.

"I'll get you a new one," she said. "There's a place in Halifax does a good one, proper cotton, and you can have it for your birthday and there's an end of it."

"No," said Sylvia.

"Mother —"

"No." Not loud. Not sharp. She said it the way you put your hand flat on a door somebody is trying to open. After a second Alison stopped pushing, because she had been pushing at that door for fifty-two years and it had never once moved.

"Let me have it, then, and I'll do the cuffs."

"You can do the cuffs."

She brought it home on the bus on her knee. She had the thread out on the table by nine, and the good needle, and the bit of matching she had been carrying in her box since about 2004 for exactly this.

She did not do it.

She sat with a cup of tea going cold and did not do it, and then she put the coat over the back of the kitchen chair to be getting on with tomorrow.

It stopped there all evening. From the doorway, in the half-light off the street, it was the shape of a woman sat with her back to you, her shoulders exactly so, and the room going quiet around her.
chapters.cliffhanger: Her mother would like to know what she is now, and will keep asking until she is told.

chapters.title: Someone Else's Chalk
chapters.segment_text:
## Chapter 7 — Someone Else's Chalk

The dress came in on the Tuesday with a woman who wanted it taking in at the waist and had a wedding in Skipton on the third.

Navy, lined, good enough cloth. Alison turned the collar to look for a label out of habit, and there it was, cream with a gold edge and the copperplate E. Ellerby's of Ravensgate. Est. 1904.

"Bought it there," the woman said. "Six year back, seven. Had it altered there and all. I'd have took it back but —" and she made a small movement of the hand that took in the whole of Corn Street.

"Let's see it on."

She saw it on, and pinned it, and wrote the ticket, and the woman went off to Bernie's for a pie.

Then she turned it inside out.

The seam had been let out at some point, by somebody who knew what they were about — old stitch line pressed flat, new one running true, allowance opened and laid down. And there on the wrong side, an inch below the waist, was a chalk mark. Two strokes and a small firm tick, the tick going away to the left and up, put there by a left hand.

Alison sat down.

She knew that hand at fifty paces. Nineteen years of it: on tickets, on the pad by the kettle, on the back of a fag packet in 2010 when the two of them had worked out between them whether Pauline could afford a caravan. Two strokes and a tick that went the wrong way, because everything Pauline did went the wrong way and came out right.

2019. She could nearly do the year off the cloth. She could nearly do the month.

They had sat three feet apart, Pauline on the window side. Pauline had known in January. She had sat on the staff consultation panel and been given a form of words, and had gone on saying good morning, and how's your Joe, and I'll put the kettle on, from January to the fourteenth of April, when the rest of them found out with the local paper. It was not a lie. Alison had been over it enough times to be sure of that. It was a silence, and a silence is worse. You cannot hold it up and say look what she's done. There is nothing in your hands.

She had not rung. Pauline had not rung. That was the twenty-first week of it.

She did the work. She unpicked the old seam and took it in the inch and a quarter it wanted and pressed it, and the whole afternoon her fingers went over that chalk line and either side of it, and she did not rub it out. It would have taken a thumb.

At half three she pressed the new seam and turned the dress the right way out, and the chalk went where the allowance went — folded in, flat to the inside of a seam that nobody would now ever open again.
chapters.cliffhanger: She has not spoken to Pauline Craddock since the fourteenth of April, and Pauline has not rung either.

chapters.title: Bernie's Pocket
chapters.segment_text:
## Chapter 8 — Bernie's Pocket

Bernie Fazakerley came down the hall on Thursday morning with her tabard over her arm and the biro behind her ear, saying, before she had arrived, "Now then. You'll not do owt with this."

The right pocket had come off. Not torn — come off, the whole of it, leaving its own shape behind in a paler blue, because forty years of a hand going in and out of a pocket is forty years of a hand going in and out of a pocket, and cloth is only cloth.

"I've had this tabard since our Denise were at school," Bernie said. "She's forty-one."

"It's had a life."

"It's had a better one than me."

Alison put her hand flat inside and felt the cloth where the pocket had been, and it was thin as a page. Bernie gave her, unasked, the history of the hall: who had been on pitch 11 before her, which was a fishmonger, and what became of him, which was Blackpool.

"I'll want to double it," Alison said. "Put a facing in behind, or it'll go again in a fortnight."

"Do what you like, love. What's the damage?"

"Six pound."

Bernie made a noise like a kettle taken off early and went up the hall, and came back four minutes later with a steak pie on a paper bag and set it down on the ticket.

"Bernie —"

"You've been here a week."

"It's not a week, it's —"

"You've been here a week," said Bernie, in the voice of a woman putting a lid on, "and I don't take money off anybody in their first week. Ask any of them. Ask Yusuf. Ask Kelly. It's not a rule I've made up this morning to be nice to you, it's forty year old, and I'll thank you not to be the first."

So Alison ate a steak pie standing up at eleven in the morning, with the paper bag round the bottom of it and her thumb through the crust, and somebody had made it and handed it to her, and it was the first time since April that anybody had put hot food into her hands. She did not say that. Bernie was three feet away, on to a man from the council.

The biro stayed behind her ear. When she wanted to write down what she owed the flour man she took a different one out of her apron.

Alison rebuilt the pocket after dinner. She cut a facing from a bit of blue drill out of her own box and set it in behind, and squared the pocket up and bar-tacked both corners the way you do a work pocket. And then, because the tabard was on her table and Bernie was fifty feet away with her back to her, she made it an inch deeper than it had been.

She never said. Bernie never noticed. All that afternoon her hand went in and out of it, down to the knuckle, as though it had always been that deep, and had always fit.
chapters.cliffhanger: Somebody has left a wedding dress on her table with no name attached to it.

chapters.title: The Second Wearer
chapters.segment_text:
## Chapter 9 — The Second Wearer

The dress was on the table when she opened up on Saturday, in a zipped carrier with no name on it, and nobody in the hall knew a thing about it — which in that hall meant somebody knew everything about it and had been asked not to say.

Alison unzipped it two inches and left it.

The young woman came at twenty past ten. Thirty-four, and she stood at the end of the table with her keys still in her hand.

"That's mine. Sorry. Hilary let me leave it. I wasn't sure I'd come."

"Well, you have."

Ivory duchesse satin, a wedding dress, 1985, made by somebody in a room with a wireless on. Long sleeves, a covered button placket to the waist, a bit of yellow at the neck where a neck had been.

"It's my mum's."

"It's lovely."

"She's fine. She's not — sorry. Everybody thinks. She's in Brighouse, she's fine, she got it down out the loft in March and said have it if you want it." The girl was talking very fast. "And I put it on. And it doesn't. I got the sleeves on. I couldn't do the back. And I've said to Craig, we'll just buy one, it's daft, and he says get it altered, and I says you can't just —"

"Take your coat off," Alison said, "and let's have a look at it inside out."

She turned the dress and laid it flat on the deal, wrong side up, and opened the back seams with her thumbs, and looked.

"Right," she said, in the voice she used for a job. "Whoever made this left an inch and a quarter down both back seams and another inch at the side. That's two and a half inch, and it's never been touched. And there's a full inch in the sleeve head, which nobody does now."

"So it'd —"

"There's plenty here," Alison said. "There's plenty here. They left plenty. It's a job of about four hours."

And the girl's shoulders came down. Not a bit of the way. Two inches, all at once, the way a curtain drops when you take the rod out — and she stood in the draught of the north door and let go of a breath she had been holding somewhere up near her ears since March.

Nobody said anything about her body. Not one word. There was a dress with an inch and a quarter in the back seams and a woman who wanted to wear it, and those are two facts about cloth.

"Come Tuesday," Alison said. "Bring your shoes."

When she had gone, Alison lifted the dress by the shoulders and held it up to the glass in the north door, and read the old allowance through the satin — a shadow, a darker band, a hand's width of cloth folded in and left there forty-one years ago by a woman at a machine who had never met this girl, and who had left her room anyway.
chapters.cliffhanger: In the morning there is a woman waiting at the north door in a suit she bought in 2009.

chapters.title: The Suit
chapters.segment_text:
## Chapter 10 — The Suit

She was at the north door before Alison had the cover off the machine, in the suit, holding her handbag in front of her with both hands.

"I'm ever so sorry. I'm early. Sorry. Are you even open? Sorry. I'll come back — sorry."

"That's four," Alison said. "Come in out of the draught."

Forty-nine. The suit was black, bought in 2009, worn twice: a funeral, and a do at a hotel where her husband's firm gave him a glass thing with his name spelled wrong on it. Thursday she had an interview. Office manager, a haulage firm, twenty-eight hours.

"It'll not fit right," she said. "I'm not the same as I was in 2009, am I. Nobody is."

"Nobody is," Alison agreed, and got her tape. "Stand normal. Don't stand nice for me. Stand how you stand."

The woman stood how she stood, which took her a moment to find.

"Eleven year I've been out," she said, to the room. "I did my mum, at the end. Four year of that. Before that it were the kids. And they give you a form, and the box says employment history. Eleven year of my life and there's nowt goes in the box."

Alison had four pins in her mouth, which was fortunate, because what she wanted to say was that she had spent twenty-six years being extremely good at a thing the world had decided was not a profession, and that there was no box on any form for that either.

"Sorry," the woman said. "You don't want all this."

"That's five," said Alison.

The trouble was the shoulder. It was a 2009 shoulder, sitting a good inch out past where the woman actually was, so that the whole suit hung off her like a coat off a chair back.

"Can you not just let it out somewhere?"

"There's nowt wrong wants letting out. It's sat out here" — she put two fingers on the seam — "and it wants to sit here. I'll take the shoulder in and lift the sleeve head half an inch. That's the whole job."

"That's all?"

"That's all there is."

She did it that morning and had her back at two. There was no mirror at the table, so she walked her down the hall to Sonia's, where there is a long one screwed to the drawers, and Sonia moved a box of bias binding off the floor in front of it without being asked.

The woman looked at herself.

And she came up. Nobody told her to. Her chin came up and her shoulders went back, and she stood on a Monday morning and looked at somebody she appeared to recognise.

She said nothing. Alison said nothing. Sonia, four feet away, said nothing at all, which for Sonia was a considerable amount of saying.

"Right," the woman said, at last.

"Right," said Alison.
chapters.cliffhanger: Somebody is coming with curtains, and she has already said she does not do curtains.

chapters.title: Curtains
chapters.segment_text:
## Chapter 11 — Curtains

He came at twenty past ten with the curtains in two carrier bags and set them on the end of the table the way a man sets down a thing he has carried further than he meant to.

"I've been told you'll not do curtains."

"Who told you that?"

"The woman with the pies."

Alison looked at the bags. She had said it herself, on her second day, to Hilary, and had heard her own voice say it and had not stopped to look at the sound. *I don't do curtains.* There had been an edge on it. The edge had been fitted to her over twenty-six years on the fourth floor at Ellerby's, where curtains were soft furnishings and soft furnishings were not alterations, and everybody had known their place including the cloth.

She took a pair out. Lined cotton sateen, a leaf pattern in green and rust, chosen with care in a shop in about 1998 and chosen again every morning since. The drop was six inches out, perhaps seven.

"They came with the house?"

"They came with the window. New window, March. Fella took the old one out and the new one sits higher." He put his hands in his coat pockets. "So they've been down on the floor since. I've not moved owt in that room since March." He stopped. "I thought I'd start with the curtains."

Alison did not ask. She measured instead, along the table, then on her knees for the second pair, and wrote the drop on the back of a docket and read it out to him, and he said that sounded about right.

"Thirty-eight pounds," she said. "For the four. There's the lining to do as well as the face, and the weights to come out and go back in."

She made herself say the number with nothing on the end of it. It sat in the air of the hall, naked, and she did not go after it with a *but if that's too much*. He took out his wallet and counted three tens, a five and three pound coins onto the deal, the way you pay for a thing that costs what it costs.

"Thursday," she said.

"No rush." And then, at the north door: "There is a bit of a rush, actually. It's dark at teatime now."

There was no room on the table to check the hang, so she laid the first pair on the floor of the hall, six feet of lining on cold stone under the lanterns, and knelt at the top of it with her chalk. She was aware of being looked at. She carried on. Kelly, without a word and without stopping the milk she was steaming, put one hand on the end of the coffee cart and walked it eighteen inches towards pitch 7, and stood a bit narrower behind it for the rest of the day, and never mentioned it.

Alison worked from the floor with the chalk in her teeth. She was furious. Not with him. With the fourth floor, and with every hem she had ever priced at what she thought a woman would put up with.
chapters.cliffhanger: The lad with the football shirt will not say who signed it.

chapters.title: The Shoulder
chapters.segment_text:
## Chapter 12 — The Shoulder

He was nineteen and he had the shirt inside his coat rather than in a bag, which told her most of it before he opened his mouth.

"Sleeve's gone," he said. "There." He laid it out and turned it so the shoulder faced her, and put a finger near it and not on it.

A Town shirt, blue and white, the badge lifting at one corner. The seam at the sleeve-head had let go for four inches, the thread perished the way thread does when a shirt has been folded on the same fold for years. And across the shoulder, in marker faded from black to a warm brown, a signature: a great confident loop and a line ruled under it that ran nearly to the collar.

The ink crossed the seam. Of course it did.

"Who signed it?"

He looked at the badge. "Just someone."

"Right."

She turned it inside out and worked her thumb along the split. If she closed that seam the ordinary way, the needle would go through the tail of the signature nine times, and the marker would craze along the stitch line, and in a year the loop would have a dotted line through it like a coupon. She sat back and had a think, with her thumb going against her forefinger.

What she did in the end took fifty minutes. She dropped the sleeve out of the armhole entirely, which is not what you do, and worked from the wrong side with the shoulder laid flat over a rolled towel so the ink never came under tension. She used a fine ballpoint needle and shortened the stitch, and stopped a quarter-inch shy of the letters and picked the last of it up by hand from the reverse, catching one thread of the jersey at a time. Small stitches. Slow ones. The kind nobody sees, which is the kind she has spent her life on.

The hall got on with itself. Yusuf's wheel. Bernie's commentary. Margo playing something dreadful.

"Is it a player?" Alison said, halfway, not looking up. "Somebody good?"

"No." A long pause. She let it be long. "It's me grandad's. He signed it for me at Shay when I were seven. I asked him for his autograph and he did it, and me mum went spare because it were a new shirt." He rubbed the back of his neck. "It's daft."

"It's not daft."

"He's in a home at Elland now. I go Sundays."

"Right," said Alison, and put the needle in again, and said nothing else, because he had not come here to be talked to.

She finished it at ten to twelve and pressed the shoulder over the ham with the iron held an inch off and the steam doing the work. The loop sat exactly where it had sat. You could not find the seam unless you knew, and she knew, and she was not going to say.

"Five pounds," she said.

He carried it to the north light and held it up by the shoulders and photographed it. Then he turned the phone the other way round and did it again, and looked at the two, and sent one.
chapters.cliffhanger: On Saturday, for the first time, there is a queue.

chapters.title: A Queue
chapters.segment_text:
## Chapter 13 — A Queue

At ten past nine there were three waiting and Alison assumed they were waiting for the cash machine by the north door, which has been broken since the spring.

They were not waiting for the cash machine.

Word had gone round. It goes round in a town that size the way water goes down a hill, by whatever route is open: the school gate, the queue at Bernie's, a woman telling another woman in the Co-op that there's a lass in the Lantern doing knees for four pound. By half past nine there were five. By ten there were eleven jobs in the building — on the table, on the floor, over the back of the chair, three of them in knotted bags with a name on a bit of paper inside, left by people who had not queued at all because they had assumed, correctly, that she would still be there.

She wrote them in a school exercise book in the hand she had used on Ellerby's dockets for twenty-six years. Name, garment, job, price, day. School trousers. A cuff. Another cuff. A zip in a fleece, which she should have refused and did not. Two prom dresses for October from the same family, the girls not speaking to one another. A pair of work trousers ripped clean across the seat, handed over folded with the rip turned in by a man who would not meet her eye, and she took them and said nothing at all and put three pounds in the book, and that was the correct thing to do.

The heat came at half past ten, the way it did now, arriving without knocking. Alison put the needle down before it reached her hands, because a needle does not care what your body is doing. She opened the north door two inches. Bernie, four stalls down, did not look up, and did not stop talking, and slid the little fan along the counter towards her.

By one o'clock she had stopped being frightened of the book. By two she was wrecked. Her back had gone at the top, between the shoulder blades, in the place that had had a chair fitted to it for a quarter of a century and now had a stool with no back on it. She ate half a pie standing at the machine with her left hand and could not afterwards have told anybody what was in it.

She was a business. That was the thing that sat oddly. Not that she was busy — she had always been busy; being busy had been done to her by other people since 1990. It was that the money was hers and the mistakes would be hers and the day was a thing she had made herself, out of a table nobody had wanted for two years, under the worst of the draught.

At five to four the queue was still four deep. She looked up between two hems to see how much of it was left, and at the end of it, patient, in her coat, with the ring of thirty-one keys in her hand and not a stitch of anything to be mended, stood Hilary Ashworth, waiting her turn.
chapters.cliffhanger: There is an envelope in Hilary's office that she has not opened for six days.

chapters.title: The Envelope
chapters.segment_text:
## Chapter 14 — The Envelope

The envelope had been on Hilary's desk since the Wednesday, propped against the tin where the fire-door keys live. She had not opened it. She had not put it in a drawer either, which Alison thought afterwards was the most honest thing about it.

Ivan Prewitt came at two. Forty-odd, in a coat bought for a different job, carrying a clipboard the way a man carries an umbrella he does not believe in. He said good afternoon to the hall in general and the hall in general looked at him.

They got twenty people into a back office with room for nine. Bernie stood in the doorway. Margo sat on the filing cabinet and did not apologise for it. Alison stood at the back by the kettle, and had a clear thought, which was that she had been trading for nineteen days and had no business being in this room, and stayed.

He read out numbers he had not written. That was the thing she could not stop noticing: the man was reading. Thirty-one pitches. Twenty-two let. A footfall figure from a count done on a wet Tuesday in February, which Bernie had views on. The roof: eleven lanterns, four of them gone, a leak over pitch 7 that had been on a list since 2019 and had rained on Ken's cards for seven winters. Fourteen months remaining on the lease. And an operator — he used that word, operator, twice, and heard himself use it the second time — interested in the ground floor. Which was to say the hall. Which was to say all of them.

"Interested in what way?" said Sonia.

"Flexible retail and leisure."

"What's that when it's at home?"

"I don't know," Ivan said. "I genuinely don't. It's not my wording."

And he put the sheet down on the desk, face up, so anybody could read it, which was not what a man defending a document does.

Nobody shouted. Alison had expected shouting and there was none, and the absence of it was worse. Margo asked what date. Yusuf asked, very quietly, whether a decision had been taken already and they were being told, and Ivan said no, and then said, more slowly, that he could not promise what a committee would do in fourteen months but that nothing had been decided, and that he would rather say that than say something comfortable.

Hilary said almost nothing. She read the lease clause he pointed at, aloud, in a voice that gave nothing away, the way she reads everything.

Alison stood by the kettle with her thumb going against her forefinger. Nineteen days. She had a table, and a book with eleven jobs in it, and a hall that had started saying her name without her surname, and a hot pie once a week she was not allowed to pay for, and the whole of it had a date on it now, the way the fourth floor had had a date on it, and nobody had told her that either until April.

When the room emptied, Hilary put her keys down on the desk between them. Thirty-one, on a steel ring. Three of them open nothing at all.
chapters.cliffhanger: A woman is coming in the morning with a dress she cannot fasten, and it has been in the boot of her car for a year.

chapters.title: Seam Allowance
chapters.segment_text:
## Chapter 15 — Seam Allowance

The dress came in a carrier bag that had been folded down and folded down again over a year, until the top of it had gone soft and grey as a dishcloth.

"It's been in the boot," the woman said. Fifty-five or so, good coat, and she said it lightly, in the voice of somebody delivering a line she has practised in a car. "I don't know what I think's going to happen to it. I've ruined it, is what it is."

Alison took it out. Green — a proper green, wool crepe with weight in it — bought in 2019 for a day that had mattered, which she knew because nobody drives a dress about for a year over a day that did not.

"What is it you can't do with it?"

"It won't fasten," the woman said, and laughed.

Alison turned the dress inside out on the table. She laid the side seam flat under her hand and ran her thumb — the flat one, the one that has been pushing a needle since 1990 — down the pressed-open allowance from the arm to the hip.

An inch and a half. Both sides. Folded in, pressed, overlocked at the raw edge and left there by somebody in a factory on a machine running at eight hundred stitches a minute, who had never met this woman and never would.

"Come and look at this," Alison said.

The woman came round the table, which people do not do.

"That's your seam allowance." She held it open with two fingers so the light came through the weave. "Inch and a half each side. That's three inch across the body of the dress, sat there in the cloth. It's been in there the whole time it's been in your boot."

"Is that not a mistake?"

"It's the opposite of a mistake." Her voice went plain, the way it goes when she is telling somebody a true thing about cloth, which is the only kind of thing she has ever been entirely sure of. "It costs them cloth to leave it and they leave it anyway. Because a maker leaves you room. Bodies alter. That's not a fault in the body, that's a fact about bodies, and a maker who knows her trade puts an inch and a half in the seam and says nowt about it." She let the cloth fall closed. "Nobody's body is a monument. It's not meant to stand still."

She took the dress to the machine and did not turn round for a moment.

Because it had gone through her, standing under eleven panes of glass with the green in her hands. Her own body had been altering itself these two years without a fitting. Nobody had chalked the line. Nobody had asked her to stand still. She had left room for every woman in this town and none whatever for herself.

It took forty minutes. The woman put it on behind Sonia's curtain and came out and fastened it, in the north light, and did not look at the mirror at all.

She looked at Alison.

And Alison, who has done this ten thousand times, turned to the machine and found something to do with her hands.
chapters.cliffhanger: Sonia Aktar's father's shears have not been out of their cloth since 2011.

chapters.title: The Yard Measure
chapters.segment_text:
## Chapter 16 — The Yard Measure

Sonia asked her at ten to nine, before the doors went up, which was itself a piece of information.

"Six kameez," she said. "My cousin's daughter. Eleven days."

"Who's doing them?"

"You are. I'll finish. My auntie was cutting and my auntie's hands have gone."

Alison heard herself say that she did alterations. She heard how it came out. It came out exactly like *I don't do curtains*, and she stood in her own draught with the sound of it and was ashamed in a way that had nothing to do with Sonia.

"I've not cut anything from flat since the bridal shop," she said. "That's twenty-six year."

"Twenty-six years of taking things apart," said Sonia. "You'll know how they go together."

Which was true and was not the point. To mend is to be handed a thing that already exists; whatever shape it is, the shape is not your fault. To cut is to decide. Alison had spent a lifetime being unable to be blamed and had not noticed until that minute that this was what it was.

"Right," she said. "Bring us the cloth."

Sonia went behind the counter and came back with a bolt of shot silk the colour of a wet slate roof, and then went again and came back with something else: a bundle of grey cloth, tied with tape, about eighteen inches long. She put it on the counter and unwrapped it without ceremony.

Shears. Black-handled, heavy, the blades long and blued at the shoulder.

"My father's," Sonia said. "He wrapped them in 2011. He sharpened them first. He knew he wasn't going to use them again, so he sharpened them, and then he put them away."

Alison did not pick them up straight off. She looked at them for a second on the counter and then she took them, and they sat in her hand with all their weight in the right place, the way a good tool does, so that they seemed to want to be closed.

They started at four, when the Saturday thinned. The hall went home around them by degrees — Kelly's shutter, Yusuf's wheel stopping, Margo's records going into their box with a noise like a deck of cards. Bernie came past at half five with two teas and no comment, which from Bernie is a bouquet. Hilary locked the north door and left the small one, and said, on her way out, that the lights over pitch 4 wanted an hour on the clock, and did not turn them off.

By seven there were two lamps on in the whole building and everything else was the black of glass at night. Six kameez, cut and stacked, the sleeves paired and pinned, the necks marked. Alison's knees had an opinion about the floor and her thumb had another and she had ignored both since half four.

Sonia measured a length off against the counter without looking down, thumb landing on the brass at thirty-six inches, where the metal has been worn to a shine by seventy years of thumbs — her father's, and his father's, and now, on the same inch, warm from the same shine, Alison's.
chapters.cliffhanger: Margo Denby needs something to wear on Wednesday, and will not say what for.

chapters.title: Margo's Green
chapters.segment_text:
## Chapter 17 — Margo's Green

"It's got to be Wednesday," Margo said, and put the frock on the table like a woman laying down a hand of cards.

It was green. Not the green of the columns, and not the green of Margo's thumbnail either; a hot, ringing, absolutely unrepentant green, cut in 1971 by somebody who had never heard of restraint, with a fitted bodice and a seam up the back you could have hung a door on.

"That is a frock," said Alison.

"That is a frock," Margo agreed. "I wore it eleven months. Every night for eleven months and twice on a Saturday, and it went in a case at the end of it and it's been in the case since, and now I want it on Wednesday."

"For what?"

"For Wednesday."

Alison let it go and picked the frock up instead, and turned it, and found what she had known she would find: the maker had been mean. Half an inch at the sides, if that. Whatever came out of this frock was going to have to come from somewhere else.

"There's not much in the seams," she said. "I can have the back seam over — move it entirely, take it out and set it again a full inch to the left, and let the sides go as far as they'll go. It'll want a new zip."

"Do it."

"You'll be a different shape in the back than you were."

"Love," said Margo, "I'm a different shape in the back than I was."

It took forty minutes and Margo talked for all of them. The band. Eleven months, 1971, a van with a hole in the floor you could watch the A62 through. Doncaster. A man from a record company who had, according to Margo, wept. She had sung, apparently, to nine hundred people in Sheffield, and then, when Alison put a pin in her mouth and raised an eyebrow, to something under two hundred, and then, after a while, said the true bit, quietly, with her hand flat on the cloth: that there had been four of them and they had been good, actually. Properly good. For about eleven months they had been the best thing in any room they walked into.

"Where are they now?"

"Dead, two of them. Barry's in Spain, which is worse." A beat. "It's Ray's on Wednesday. Rochdale. He played bass and he could not play bass, and I've decided I'm going in this, and they can all think what they like."

Alison put a pin in and said nothing and let the machine say it instead. The zip went in at twenty past. She pressed the new back seam over the ham and hung it on the hook by the north door, where the light gets it.

Margo stood and looked at it for a while with her arms folded. She put her hand out and took a fold of the skirt between finger and thumb — the chipped green nail against the green cloth, and the two greens not agreeing in any particular whatsoever, not one atom of them the same green.

"I'm aware," she said.
chapters.cliffhanger: There is a blazer in the bag with a name tape in it that is not anybody's name any more.

chapters.title: A Name Tape
chapters.segment_text:
## Chapter 18 — A Name Tape

Wednesday is half-day, so by one the hall had gone soft and echoing, the shutters coming down in ones and twos, Yusuf's wheel silent, Bernie counting the float out loud four stalls away because Bernie does everything out loud.

They came at ten past twelve: a mother in her forties and a fourteen-year-old in a coat with the sleeves over their hands. The blazer came out of a bag and went on the table.

"It's too big round the middle," the mother said. "It's been too big since we bought it. And there's — " she turned the collar over — "there's a tape in there."

Alison put her glasses on and got in under the lantern light. Woven tape, sewn into the neck facing with the small, tight, over-and-over hand of somebody who had been shown once and got it right. A name.

"Right," said Alison. "Two jobs, then. Waist and a tape."

"Yes," said the mother.

There is a question that belongs to Alison and a great many questions that do not, and thirty-six years at other people's shoulders had taught her the difference, which is not a thing you can be taught in a morning. She did not ask the ones that were not hers.

She looked at the fourteen-year-old, who was looking at the floor.

"What am I putting on the new one?" she said.

They told her.

"And how do you spell it?"

They spelled it. Alison wrote it on the docket in pencil, in capitals, and turned the docket round on the table so it faced them, the way she had turned ten thousand dockets round.

"Like that?"

"Yeah."

"Right."

She did the waist first, because it was the bigger job and the machine makes a noise, and a noise is somewhere to put a silence. Two inches out of the back seam, tapered, with the vent kept true — a blazer will forgive you a lot and will not forgive you a crooked vent — and the lining eased and dropped so it hung free, which is what a lining is for, so the outside can move without being told about it by the inside.

Then the tape. She unpicked the old one with the point of the quick-unpick, one stitch at a time, and it took longer than sewing it had, because that is the arithmetic of unpicking. It came away whole. She laid it on the table.

She sewed the new tape in with silk thread and did the ends first so it could not pull, and did over-and-over, small and tight, the same stitch that was already there, because there was no reason to do it differently and every reason not to.

"Six pound," she said. "Try it before you go."

They put it on. It fitted at the waist. They did up the button and put their hands in the pockets and stood there.

The mother picked the old tape up off the table, and folded it once, and put it in her purse, behind a card, and pressed the purse shut with both thumbs.

Alison saw her do it, and got on with clearing the table, and did not mention it. Not then. Not ever.
chapters.cliffhanger: The Singer has been making a noise since Tuesday, and this morning it stops.

chapters.title: The Motor
chapters.segment_text:
## Chapter 19 — The Motor

It had been making a noise since Tuesday — a small dry chirp at the top of the stroke, once every four or five inches of seam, that she had heard and had decided to hear later.

On Friday at twenty past nine it stopped. Not the noise. The machine.

She did the things you do. Plug, socket, the socket that Kelly's cart uses, the pedal, the pedal again, the belt, the belt tension, the plug once more because you always do the plug twice. The Singer sat on the deal in the north light, black and gold and older than she was and utterly finished with the whole business.

Alison stood behind her table and understood, in about the time it takes to boil a kettle, exactly what she was: a woman of fifty-two with a book of eleven jobs, seventy-two pounds a week going out, a redundancy she had promised herself she would not eat, and one machine. There was a new one in a shop in Halifax for four hundred pounds that was plastic and did a hundred stitches she would never use. She had a think about four hundred pounds. She did not like the think.

Yusuf came at half nine, because Bernie had told him, because Bernie tells everybody everything.

He did not ask. He put both arms round the machine, lifted it off the table with his knees and not his back, and carried it the length of the hall to pitch 19 with his chin over the balance wheel, and Alison walked behind it carrying the pedal and the flex.

He spread a sheet of newspaper. He took the plate off the end of the motor with a screwdriver he did not have to look for. Inside it was black — carbon dust, years of it, packed in the corners like soot in a flue. He blew it out. He turned the armature with one finger and listened, head over on one side, the way he listens to a key on the wheel.

"Brush," he said.

He held it up. A little block of carbon on a spring, worn down past its own shoulder to a stub the size of a back tooth, its spring gone slack behind it, no longer able to reach the thing it had been touching since 1949.

"It is one pound sixty," he said. "I have three."

"Yusuf."

"One pound sixty," he said, and would not be moved, and did not look up, and started cleaning the commutator with a scrap of emery on the end of a lolly stick.

He was forty minutes. He carried it back. She plugged it in and put a doubled scrap of calico under the foot and ran a seam, and it went, and it went sweet — the long low note it had had at Ellerby's under the north window, the note she had heard eight hours a day for twenty-six years and had stopped hearing about 2004.

Yusuf stood with his head on one side and listened for about four inches of it.

Then he nodded, before the seam had finished, and went back to pitch 19.
chapters.cliffhanger: On Saturday the traders are meeting in the hall after closing, and everybody has been asked.

chapters.title: A Show of Hands
chapters.segment_text:
## Chapter 20 — A Show of Hands

They put forty chairs out and twenty-two people came, which meant that for the whole of it there were eighteen empty chairs in the middle of the hall, and nobody sat on the front row, so it looked worse than it was.

Hilary had the urn on. Kelly had turned her chalkboard round and wiped the back of it, so that CAMOMILE was facing the wall, still spelled wrong, waiting.

Bernie went first and spoke for nine minutes. Nine. Alison timed it in the end because she had nothing else to do with her eyes. It was about her father-in-law, and the fish stall that used to be at pitch 11, and a man from the council in 1994 who had said a thing that had turned out not to be true, and somewhere in the middle of it there was one hard sentence — *they've been letting the roof go for eleven years and nobody's daft* — that nobody picked up, because it had nine minutes wrapped round it.

Margo proposed that they stop paying rent and put it in a jar until the roof was done. Hilary said that this was called withholding and had a legal meaning and would end the lease inside a month. Margo said she was aware. Somebody at the back said they should get the paper in. Somebody else said the paper was owned by the same lot.

Hilary read the lease out. Clause by clause, in the voice she reads everything in, which gives you nothing to lean on. Fourteen months. Break clause. Schedule of condition. The word *dilapidations*, which arrived in the hall like a stone through the glass and which four people asked about at once.

It was a mess. Alison sat at the end of the third row with her coat on and her hands in her sleeves and thought: this is what it looks like. Nobody stands up and says the thing. There is no thing. There are twenty-two people who are tired and it is quarter past eight and the urn has gone cold.

And then Sonia, who had not spoken, said, from the side, not standing up:

"They're not taking it off us. They're waiting for us to not want it."

The hall stopped.

Not dramatically. It was more that the noise in it changed key. Bernie, who had an answer to everything, did not have one. Yusuf turned round. Hilary put the lease down flat on her knee and looked at Sonia for a good three seconds and did not say a word, which from Hilary was the loudest thing that happened all night.

They stayed. That was the strange part. Somebody found the urn a plug that worked. At nine the lanterns went off because they are on a timer and nobody had the key for the timer, and the hall filled up instead with the orange of the streetlight on Corn Street coming down through eleven panes of dirty Victorian glass, and by that light, twenty-two people went on standing about in their coats, arguing, not leaving.

Alison was at the north door with her bag at ten past nine when she saw her.
chapters.cliffhanger: Pauline Craddock is at the north door at ten past nine, holding something she should not have.

chapters.title: Left-Handed Scissors
chapters.segment_text:
## Chapter 21 — Left-Handed Scissors

On the Saturday night she had come as far as the north door and no further.

Alison was stacking chairs six high, the way you learn to in a building with no storeroom, and she turned with one in each hand and there Pauline Craddock was, in the orange of the streetlight, holding a carrier bag against her front with both arms. The way you hold a bag when what is in it is heavier than the bag.

"Tuesday," Pauline said, through the gap. "When it's quiet."

"Right."

"I'm not doing this in front of Bernie Fazakerley."

She came at twenty past eleven on the Tuesday, which is the deadest hour the Lantern has. Bernie was at her ovens. Margo had a man at pitch 2 wanting something by Hot Chocolate. Kelly put two teas on the corner of the table without being asked and went back to her cart and stayed at it, which was, from Kelly, an act of considerable self-denial.

Pauline put the bag down and took out a stick of tailor's chalk and set it between them. Square-edged, blue paper sleeve, one corner rounded off by a thumb. Then the scissors. Left-handed, black japanned, red insulating tape round the bow gone tacky the way that tape goes.

"They'd have skipped the lot," Pauline said.

"They did skip the lot."

"Well then."

Under the chalk, the table's ghost sign said T. CRABTREE & SON · NOTHING OVER 50p. Both of them looked at it rather than at each other.

"I knew in January," Pauline said.

"I know."

"I'd signed a thing."

"I know that an' all."

"They give you the wording." Pauline turned the chalk a quarter-turn on the deal with one finger, squaring it to the edge, the way she had squared everything for nineteen years. "You sit in a room and they give you the wording and tell you what you can say and what you can't, and you think, right, I'll manage that. Then Monday you're stood three foot from her doing a hem, and she says are you all right, love, and you say I'm all right."

"Eleven weeks."

"Eleven weeks." She looked at her hands. "I could have rung you in April."

"You didn't ring me in April."

"No."

"I didn't ring you either."

Pauline said she had walked past the north door most weeks since the second one. Alison said she knew; Bernie had told her. Pauline said that Bernie told everybody everything, and Alison said that she did, and that was the nearest either of them came to the word sorry, and it did the job.

Then Pauline picked the scissors up, and for a moment Alison thought she was taking them back. She turned them round and laid them down again on Alison's side of the table, handle towards her, blades away, the way you pass a thing to somebody you would rather not cut.

"Your cutting was always better than mine," Pauline said. "That's not me being nice."

"I know it's not."

She did not use them that day. She sat with them by her right hand all afternoon and got a good deal done.
chapters.cliffhanger: Ivan Prewitt has a list of what is possible, and it is shorter than anybody hoped.

chapters.title: What Is Possible
chapters.segment_text:
## Chapter 22 — What Is Possible

Ivan Prewitt came on the Thursday with one sheet of A4 and no clipboard. Hilary noticed the clipboard was missing and said nothing.

They put him in the back office and left the door open, because Bernie said if he was going to say it he could say it where folk could hear it. Ivan said that was fair enough and stood in the doorway.

He read the four things out badly, the way a man reads when he has practised in the car and the practising has made it worse.

One: they would have to become a thing. A community benefit society, registered, with rules and members and a share worth a pound. Not a committee. Not a group of people who cared. A body, with a number.

Two: the council could not lease to a body that did not exist, and could — he said could twice — grant a fifteen-year lease to one that did, at a rent he would not promise and did not think would be silly.

Three: a business plan. Three years of numbers, the roof costed, the lets listed, the rent they would collect and the rent they never would. In by the twelfth of November for the committee on the second of December. Not the twelfth as in about the twelfth. The twelfth.

Four: a chair and a secretary. Names. Real ones, on a form, with addresses on them.

"That's it," he said. "That's the list."

"That's nowt," said Bernie.

"It's everything," said Sonia, from the back, and the room went quiet, because she had said her third.

Ivan folded the sheet and put it in his inside pocket, and then took it out again and left it on the table instead. He said, to nobody in particular, that he had come to fourteen of these in six years, and eleven had waited to be rescued, and he had watched the rescue not come. He said he had no vote, would not be in the room, and could not make one line of it happen; the only people who could were in this building. Then he stopped, because he had heard himself, and he was not a man who cared for the sound.

Hilary put the form on the table, and a biro on top of the form, and pushed neither of them anywhere.

"Chair," she said. "Secretary."

Nobody spoke. The urn ticked as it cooled.

"Alison," said Margo.

"No," Alison said.

"Alison."

"I've been here five weeks. I'm the newest thing in this building bar the coffee. You want somebody who's been in forty year."

"That's me," said Bernie, "and I'm not doing it."

"Ask Sonia. Ask Hilary. Ask Yusuf, he's more sense than the lot of us." She got her coat off the hook. "I mend things. I'm not standing up in front of anybody."

She went out past the form and past the pen with one arm in her sleeve and the other still hunting for it, and got all the way to the north door before she noticed that nobody had said her name again. She was glad of that, and should not have been.
chapters.cliffhanger: They have put her name down anyway.

chapters.title: Six Needles
chapters.segment_text:
## Chapter 23 — Six Needles

The lamp came from the Argos on Corn Street and cost twenty-nine pounds. It had a bendy neck, a ring of little daylight bulbs and a shade the colour of a hospital, and it was the best money she had ever spent, including the machine.

What she had not told anybody — not Sonia, not her mother, and certainly not Pauline — was that since last winter the eye of a needle at half past six had stopped being a hole and become a rumour. She had taken to threading five at a time in the morning and lining them up in the cloth like a little fence, and calling it efficiency.

Under the lamp, the eye was a hole again. She put a size nine through at twenty to seven, first go, and had to stand still a second, holding it.

It began by accident. Kelly had asked how you do a button so it stays on, because she had one in her apron pocket since Easter, and Alison said bring it Saturday after we shut. Then the woman who had brought the school trousers in September heard, and asked if she could come, and the woman with the green dress heard from her, and two more came who Alison had never seen in her life and never did establish how they knew.

Six of them, round the Thursday table before it was the Thursday table, in a hall with the lanterns off and the rain going over the glass like a lorry that never arrives. Six holes between them: a button, a hem, two knees, a pillowcase and a moth-hole in a scarf its owner had been apologising for since she came in.

Alison had never taught anybody anything. She discovered, somewhere around the second knee, that she could — that she knew where hands go wrong before they go wrong, and could say *bring your thumb round* without making a woman feel watched, and that the trick was to say nothing and let them find the mistake themselves.

Pauline sat at the far end and did not sew. She threaded needles. Every time a woman held one up to the light and squinted, Pauline had a threaded one waiting by her elbow, and never said a word about it, and never once looked at Alison.

They ran to half eight. Kelly's button was appalling and would hold till the end of the world. The scarf woman stopped apologising at about eight and did not start again.

At the end they said, without anybody putting it to a vote, that Thursdays would be better than Saturdays, and how much did she want for it, and Alison said three pound, and they said don't be daft, and settled on five.

She walked home up Corn Street at nine with the rain on her face, and turned round at the top out of habit, to see if she had left a light on.

She had. The roof of the Lantern was glowing from the inside, all eleven lanterns of it, a long low box of light under the black hill, because six women had stayed behind to learn to do a thing with their hands.
chapters.cliffhanger: There is a jumper coming that nobody can save.

chapters.title: What Cannot Be Saved
chapters.segment_text:
## Chapter 24 — What Cannot Be Saved

She knew before it was out of the bag. After thirty-six years you know by how a thing arrives — folded, not stuffed, and the woman unfolding it herself rather than letting anybody else.

Lambswool, navy, a good one, the sort that had cost proper money in about 1998. The woman was sixty-eight and had a way of putting her hands flat on the table either side of it, as though it might go somewhere.

The moth had had it. Not one hole; a scatter across the shoulder like buckshot, and worse than the holes was what lay between them, where the cloth was eaten thin and had no purchase left. You could darn any one of those and it would tear out at the edge of your darning and take your work with it.

"Six year I've had it in that drawer," the woman said. "In a bag. With them cedar balls."

"Cedar's not much use once they're in."

"No. So I've found out."

Alison spread it and took her time. She lifted the shoulder to the north light and the light came through in a constellation, and the woman watched her do it and said nothing.

There was a version of the next minute where she had a go. Charge a tenner, spend three hours, hand back a jumper with a dozen navy dots in it that would open at the first wash, and the woman would say thank you, and would know.

"I can't save it, love," Alison said. "There's nowt left to sew to."

The woman nodded once. "I know. I knew when I got it out. I just wanted it saying by somebody that knows."

Alison turned it over.

"There's four good inches at the ribbing," she said. "The cuffs are sound — they never touch cuffs, moth, I've never worked out why, they've got standards. And that right sleeve's clean from the elbow down."

"What's that in aid of?"

"Mittens. Give us your hands."

The woman put her hands up, palms out, like a child at the sink, and Alison took the tape across her knuckles and wrote the number down.

"Two pair," she said. "There's enough for two. One for you and one for whoever you like."

The first cut is the one. She made it on the Monday afternoon with the hall going on round her, and it went through the sleeve with a small dry noise, and after that it was only work. The ribbing did for the wrists, which is what ribbing is for. She lined the palms with navy jersey off Sonia's remnant shelf that was not the same navy and did not need to be.

They took her an hour and forty minutes. The woman came back at four.

"What do I owe you?"

"Twelve pound."

She paid it in coins out of a purse with a clasp, and neither of them said the word husband, all the way through, from start to finish.

Then she took one mitten out of the bag and put it on, there, in the hall, in October, indoors — worked her fingers into it and made a fist and opened it again — and left it on.
chapters.cliffhanger: There is a parcel from Glasgow on the step, addressed in her son's handwriting.

chapters.title: Glasgow, By Post
chapters.segment_text:
## Chapter 25 — Glasgow, By Post

It had been on the step since Monday, keeping dry under the meter box, addressed in biro in a hand that had not improved since it was eleven. Postage six pounds forty. He could have got the train for less if he had wanted to, and he had not wanted to, and she was not going to pretend she did not know that.

Wednesday is half-day. She was home by two with the sun not yet round to the front room — it comes about four, over the roof of the old Co-op, and gives you an hour and then thinks better of it.

Inside the parcel, a jacket. Dark grey, half-decent, from a shop she had never heard of, folded by somebody who had never in his life been shown how. A note on the back of a receipt: *Mum. Interview Monday. Sleeves are miles too long, they're all too long, I don't know why. Don't do owt daft. J.*

The sleeves were two inches too long. They are always two inches too long; he has his father's arms and none of his father's shoulders.

She did them from the head, which is the long way and the right way, because the cuffs had working buttonholes and she was not going to be the woman who butchers a working cuff. She unpicked the lining, dropped the sleeve out, took the two inches off the top, marked the balance, put it back. An hour. A little over, with the pressing.

Then she sat with it on her knee for another one, which is not a thing she could have accounted for to anybody.

The front room went gold at about four and then stopped. On the arm of the chair was her phone with a photograph on it from Sunday, of a plate of something with a fried egg on top, sent at eleven at night with no message, because a message would have been a whole thing and a photograph is not.

Before she taped it up she took a spare button out of her tin, one of the four he had not lost yet, and sewed it inside the pocket, low in the corner, where a hand would find it in about nine years and not know how it got there. Her mother had done that to every coat she ever owned. She had never mentioned it and neither had Sylvia.

She wrote on the back of his own note, because he had left her nowt else to write on: *Sleeves done. Press it from the wrong side with a cloth, not the right side, you'll shine it. Ring your nan, she's asking. Mum.*

At the post office on Corn Street the woman weighed it and said seven pounds and ten, and Alison paid it without comment, and stood a second at the counter looking at the parcel with her own handwriting on it now, going the other way, four hundred miles, to a room she had never seen.

"Anything of value?" said the woman.

"No," said Alison. "Nowt at all."
chapters.cliffhanger: Her mother has decided the raincoat is done for, and Alison has decided otherwise.

chapters.title: Relined
chapters.segment_text:
## Chapter 26 — Relined

The concession came on the phone on the Sunday, sideways, at the end of nine minutes about the bowls committee. *That coat's had it. I'm not being told. It's had it.* Which meant: come and get it.

Alison took it apart on the Wednesday, to the last seam. That is not a figure of speech. She unpicked the lining out whole and pressed it flat and used it as her pattern, because whoever cut it in 1987 or thereabouts had cut it properly, and there is no sense being clever with a thing that already works. The wadding at the cuffs had gone to powder. The beige outer she did not touch at all, beyond a press: it is worn to the weight of paper, and the paper is the point.

New lining in a dull bronze from Sonia's rack, which was not what was in it and was what should have been. New cuffs, faced back so they would go another ten year. The shape exactly as it was. If you had shown it to a stranger they would have said nothing had been done to it, and that would have been the compliment.

She took it up to Weaver's Rise on the Friday, on the bus, in a bag.

Sylvia put it on in her own hallway, under a light that has needed a new bulb since March, and did the belt, and put her hands in the pockets, and stood in front of the mirror she has had since 1988 — the one that came from the shop that no longer exists, the same week as the coat.

She looked at herself a long time. Longer than Alison was comfortable with. Out of the window behind her, over the wall, the crematorium car park, which she has more than once described as handy.

"You've never made owt for yourself, our Alison," she said. To the mirror. Not to her. "Twenty-six year and you've never made owt for yourself."

Alison said something about the cuffs.

"I know about the cuffs. I'm saying what I'm saying."

And she did not take it back, and she did not soften it, and she did not turn round. She went into the kitchen with the coat still on and filled the kettle, and asked, over the noise of it, whether Joe had rung.

The five o'clock bus down the valley was dark and full of school kids. Alison sat halfway back with the empty bag folded on her knee and her thumb joints aching from the cold coming off the window, and did sums.

Nineteen to fifty-two. Thirty-three years. Say five hundred garments a year, some years more; call it fifteen thousand hems, and not one of them hers. She got the numbers on the window in the condensation with her finger and rubbed them out with the side of her hand before the woman next to her could see.

She had done the division without meaning to. That was the difference. This time she did not mind that she had.
chapters.cliffhanger: On Saturday the hall will know, one way or the other.

chapters.title: The Long Saturday
chapters.segment_text:
## Chapter 27 — The Long Saturday

Forty-one pages. It is worth saying what forty-one pages is made of, because nobody ever says, and it is the whole thing.

Kelly built the spreadsheet on her phone at the cart between customers over eleven days, and again on a laptop when Hilary made her. Sonia got three quotes for the roof and rang all three back to ask what they had left out, and two had left out the same thing. Bernie rang every trader who had left the hall in ten years and asked why, and wrote down what they said, and four came back and took pitches, which is on page nineteen. Yusuf costed the electrics with a man he knows in Sheffield and would not say how. Margo did nothing whatsoever and provided, she said, morale. Hilary typed it, all of it, at the desk with the fuse board humming behind her.

And Pauline read the whole thing twice, both times with a pencil, and found four errors, one a number in the wrong column that would have taken eleven thousand pounds off the rent roll and made the plan a joke. That is what nineteen years of reading other people's wording gets you. Nobody thanked her properly. She would have hated it.

The society had come through on the Thursday. A registered number in an email. Not a moment. A number.

Ivan came at two, on a Saturday, in his own time, and read it in the back office for fifty minutes with a pie he had not asked for going cold at his elbow. Then he came out and said it would go to the second of December with his recommendation to grant, and that the recommendation was worth something and was not a decision, and a committee is a committee.

"So have we got it?" said Bernie.

"No," said Ivan. "You've got a chance of it, which you didn't have in September."

And the hall cheered anyway, because you take what you are given, and because forty people had done a boring thing correctly for five weeks and there had to be a noise somewhere.

Alison had her copy on the table. Page two: the founder members, alphabetical, twelve of them. *Alison Hoyle, alterations, pitch 26.* She looked at it a while. Not long. Long enough that Sonia, going past with a box of zips, saw her looking and said nothing, which is Sonia's way of saying something.

Bernie started giving pies out at four. Not selling. Giving. She stood at pitch 11 with her arms going like a woman shovelling coal, and when Yusuf tried to put two pound on the counter she looked at it the way you look at something the cat has brought in, and he put it back in his pocket.

And Hilary took her keys out and worked the ring open with her thumbnail and took off the three that open nothing — the old cellar, the shutter that was bricked up in 1998, and one nobody has ever identified — and put them in the drawer of the desk, and shut it.

She kept the drawer. She is not a saint.
chapters.cliffhanger: The clocks go back a week on Sunday, and she has four yards of cloth to buy.

chapters.title: Four Yards
chapters.segment_text:
## Chapter 28 — Four Yards

She went to Todmorden on the Tuesday morning, on the train, four stops down the valley with the mist sitting on the water like something that had been asked to wait.

The mill shop is up an iron staircase on the outside of a building that has not made cloth since 1981. Inside it is one long room, cold, smelling of lanolin and paraffin, with the bolts standing up in rows, and a woman of about sixty at the far end with shears and a yard-rule screwed to the counter.

Alison walked it twice. She did not touch anything on the first pass, which is a discipline. On the second she put the back of her fingers to a charcoal melton, and a black that would have been a mistake and she knew it, and then she came to a grey with a green somewhere down inside it — a lichen grey, the grey of a wet slate roof at the point the sun is deciding — and she stopped.

She carried the bolt to the door. Held it up in the daylight on the iron staircase, over her arm, in the mist. Took it back inside. Held it under the strip light, which lies. Took it out again.

"It'll be the same colour when you get home," the woman said. "They never are. That one is."

"I know."

"Take it out again, then."

She took it out again.

Twenty-one pound a yard. Four yards is eighty-four pounds. She had it out of the redundancy — the redundancy she had divided on the back of an envelope in September, and been annoyed with herself for doing it — and she did not divide anything by anything. She did not work out how many knees it was, or how many hems, or how many Thursdays. Eighty-four pounds is eighty-four pounds. She stood there and let it be a number and not a verdict.

The woman got the bolt up on the counter and rolled it out along the rule, and it fell off the roll in that heavy slow way good wool has, like it is in no hurry to be anything.

She took the shears up.

And Alison heard herself say, before she could get to it, "Leave me a bit extra."

The woman did not look up and did not ask what for. She moved her hand along past the fourth yard, an inch, another half, and put the blades in there instead, and cut, and the cloth came apart with that sound, and she folded it and pressed the fold flat with the side of her fist, twice, and slid it across.

"Coat?" she said.

"Coat."

"Who for?"

There was a small pause, in a cold room, over four yards of wool, and Alison put her card on the counter with two fingers, the way you put a card down when you have decided something.

"Me," she said.
